THE SCHOOL HALL · EID · AGES 2–5

Eid — what it is and how little kids celebrate.

Eid is a joyful Muslim holiday of new clothes, sweet treats and hugs all around — “Eid Mubarak!” — and there are two every year.

Back to the Hall ↗
WHAT IS EID?

What’s this? Why do we celebrate it?

Muslim families celebrate two big holidays every year, and both are called Eid. The first, Eid al-Fitr, comes after Ramadan — a month when grown-ups fast during the day, share food with people who need it, and try to be extra kind. When Ramadan ends, the celebration bursts out: new clothes, big breakfasts, visits to family, presents and sweets for the children. The second, Eid al-Adha, comes at the time of Hajj, the great journey to the city of Makkah, and it celebrates sharing — food goes to neighbors and to families who need it most.

Both days begin the same way: dressing in new or best clothes, a special prayer, and the happy greeting that gives this page its name — “Eid Mubarak!”, which means “have a blessed Eid.” The exact date moves every year because the Islamic calendar follows the moon — the calendar above shows the expected date, and the new moon decides the rest.

TRY IT · ACTIVITIES FOR KIDS

Little hands on the big day.

Practise the greeting in the mirror until it sings: “Eid Mubarak!” Draw a crescent moon and a star and hang them in the window. Help fill a small box of treats for a neighbor — sharing food is the heart of both Eids. Dress up in your best clothes and have a little parade around the living room. And if your family has henna, one dot on a small hand is a whole adventure.
